body:
A defect in the deferred-findings retirement that #332 introduces. Filed separately rather than only noted on #332 because it is a data-loss path with its own fix, and because #332's implementation here would otherwise reproduce it faithfully — the code is already merged in the instance (getwyrd/wyrd-pdca#167) and the bug went with it.

## The defect

`autoiterate.retire_cleared` uses **two matchers of different strictness against the same data**:

- selecting an entry to retire uses the fuzzy `_same_finding`, which tolerates a human's edit to the §6 row (equality, containment, or a proportional shared opening);
- the guard that protects an entry still visibly UNCHECKED in §6 compares by **exact normalized text**.

So a human who annotates a deferred row *without* ticking it, and ticks a different but similar newly raised finding, loses the unadjudicated one:

```
ledger:  C5 Causal adequacy — guards the symptom in the parser, not the cause
§6:      - [x] C5 Causal adequacy — guards the symptom in the renderer, not the cause
         - [ ] C5 Causal adequacy — guards the symptom in the parser, not the cause (owner: architecture)

after retire_cleared -> ledger is []      # the unticked parser objection is gone
```

The annotated row no longer equals its ledger text, so the exclusion does not recognise it; the fuzzy match still selects that entry uniquely from the ticked row; the next iterate transition discards it.

## Why it survived every guard added for it

This exact loss — an unadjudicated human finding disappearing — is what the ledger exists to prevent, and it has now survived four separate hardening rounds (positive-tick-only retirement, fuzzy matching for annotated ticks, fail-closed on ambiguity, exact-match-first). Each of those made one matcher stricter or looser without touching the other.

**The guard is only ever as strong as the weaker of its two matchers**, and the weaker one is the exclusion. That asymmetry is the bug; neither matcher is wrong in isolation.

## Shape of the fix

Use the same `_same_finding` relation on both sides, so an annotated-unchecked row is recognised as the entry it protects. Carry the existing ambiguity handling over: if a ticked row and an open row both match one entry, **the open row wins** — a visible unticked box is stronger evidence than a fuzzy match.

Worth a test that asserts the two sides cannot drift apart (e.g. both routed through one predicate), since the asymmetry rather than either matcher is what recurs.

Instance issue: getwyrd/wyrd-pdca#173 — reproduced against merged instance `main`.
Introduced by: #332.

comments.body:
Milestone triage (0.56/0.57 rebalance): kept in **0.57 and blocked on #332**.

This is a real bug, but it lives entirely inside code #332 introduces — upstream the template has no `retire_cleared`, no `_same_finding`, and no deferred-findings ledger, so there is nothing here to fix until #332 lands. It was therefore not eligible for 0.56 ("all identified bugs"), which holds only bugs reachable in the template as it stands.

Practical consequence for whoever takes #332: this must be fixed **in the same change**, not after it. Porting the instance implementation faithfully reproduces the asymmetry (the fuzzy `_same_finding` selects, the exact-match exclusion protects), so the ledger ships with a data-loss path on day one. Route both sides through one predicate as described above, and land the drift test with it.

title: retire_cleared can discard an unadjudicated finding: its two matchers use different strictness

resolved.note: tracker issue closed upstream; recorded by pdca cleanup 2026-08-06
